content.title: About
content.content: Cereal, fruit crispy is a crunchy whole‑grain cereal enriched with pieces of dried fruit. It is designed for a quick breakfast, combining the sweetness of fruit with a light cereal texture.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The flakes are made from whole wheat, oat and rice grains, preserving most of their nutrients.
Dried fruits (raisins, apricots, cranberries) are added after baking to retain their aroma and vitamin content.
The product contains no artificial colourings; colour comes from natural fruit extracts.
One serving provides about 30 % of the daily recommended fiber intake.
The flakes dissolve in milk within 2–3 minutes, creating a light, airy texture.

items.title: Rich in fiber
items.content: Fiber supports digestion, promotes satiety and helps maintain healthy blood sugar levels.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Whole‑grain flakes contain thiamine, riboflavin and niacin, which are essential for energy metabolism.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Dried fruits are high in polyphenols and vitamin C, which protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Supports heart health
items.content: Whole grains provide nutrients that help maintain normal cholesterol levels.

items.title: Provides energy
items.content: Carbohydrates are quickly absorbed, making the cereal a good source of morning energy.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Dried fruits add natural sugars; people monitoring glucose should account for this in their total intake.

items.title: Cereal allergy
items.content: The product may trigger reactions in individuals allergic to wheat, oats or rice.

items.title: Gluten
items.content: The flakes contain gluten and are not suitable for a gluten‑free diet.

items.title: Possible additives
items.content: Some variants may contain flavourings or preservatives; check the label if you have sensitivities.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Pour milk or a plant‑based beverage over the flakes, wait 2–3 minutes and stir. They can also be added to yogurt, smoothies, used in baking, or as a crunchy topping for desserts.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in a cool, dry place in a sealed package. After opening, use within 4–6 weeks to keep the crunch and flavor.

content.title: About
content.content: Corn beverage is a non‑alcoholic drink made by extracting or fermenting whole corn kernels. It has a light sweet taste, a gentle aroma, and a pale yellow color. The beverage is often fortified with B‑vitamins, vitamin C, and minerals.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Corn is one of the most widely cultivated crops worldwide.
Corn beverage is traditionally popular in Latin American countries, where it is known as “aguas frescas”.
Unlike most fruit juices, plain corn beverage contains less sugar unless sweetened.
The drink can be found both carbonated and still.
Corn starch used in production gives the beverage a characteristic creamy texture.

items.title: Energy source
items.content: Carbohydrates in the drink are quickly absorbed, providing a rapid energy boost.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: Vitamins B1, B2 and B6 support metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Phenolic compounds in corn help combat free radicals.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: A modest amount of dietary fiber aids normal bowel function.

items.title: Hydration
items.content: The beverage supplies water and electrolytes, helping maintain fluid balance.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Sweetened versions can raise blood glucose levels.

items.title: Corn allergy
items.content: A small number of people may experience allergic reactions to corn proteins.

items.title: GMOs
items.content: Most commercial corn is genetically modified; choose non‑GMO if desired.

items.title: Sodium levels
items.content: Carbonated varieties sometimes contain added salt, which may be a concern for hypertension.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the corn beverage chilled as a refreshing standalone drink or use it in cocktails, smoothies, and desserts. It can also be added to marinades or sauces for a subtle sweetness.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the beverage refrigerated at 1 °C–4 °C. Once opened, consume within 3–5 days. Protect from direct sunlight.

content.title: About
content.content: Doughnuts are small fried or baked pastries made from yeast‑leavened dough (type 2834). The dough typically contains wheat flour, sugar, milk, eggs, and butter. After rising, the dough is shaped into rings or balls and fried in oil until golden, then coated with glaze, powdered sugar, or sprinkles.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Doughnuts originated in Europe in the 19th century and quickly became popular in the United States, where they are called "donuts".
Traditional preparation involves deep‑frying, but baking has become popular in recent years as a lower‑calorie alternative.
There are countless fillings: jam, custard, chocolate, caramel, and even savory options with cheese.
In Japan, colorful "pop‑mats" doughnuts covered with bright glazes and toppings are a trend.
In the U.S., the first Monday of June is celebrated as National Donut Day.

items.title: Quick energy source
items.content: Doughnuts provide rapid energy from carbohydrates, which can be useful for short‑term fuel needs.

items.title: B‑vitamin content
items.content: Yeast in the dough supplies modest amounts of B1, B2, and B6 vitamins that support metabolism.

items.title: Calcium and iron
items.content: Milk and eggs add calcium and iron, essential for bone health and blood formation.

items.title: High sugar and fat
items.content: Traditional doughnuts are rich in sugar and saturated fat, which can contribute to weight gain and elevated cholesterol.

items.title: Gluten and dairy allergies
items.content: Because the recipe uses wheat flour and milk, people with these allergies should avoid them.

items.title: Trans fats from frying
items.content: Repeated use of frying oil can create trans fats, which are harmful to cardiovascular health.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Doughnuts are usually served warm and eaten as a snack or dessert, often paired with coffee or milk. They are commonly glazed, topped with sprinkles, nuts, or filled with cream or jam.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store doughnuts in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 2 days. For longer storage, freeze them in a freezer‑safe bag for up to 2 months; reheat in an oven or microwave before eating.

content.title: About
content.content: Kohlrabi is an edible stem vegetable from the Brassicaceae family, related to cabbage, broccoli and radish. Cooked kohlrabi has a tender, mildly sweet flavor and a crisp texture. It can be boiled, stewed, roasted, or steamed.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Kohlrabi was known to the ancient Romans and used as a vegetable in Mediterranean cuisine.
The edible part is the swollen stem, not a root like most root vegetables.
Vitamin C content in kohlrabi exceeds that of oranges.
Kohlrabi comes in green and purple varieties; the color depends on the cultivar.
In Japan, kohlrabi is often served thinly sliced and pickled (tsukudani).

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C supports the immune system and aids collagen synthesis.

items.title: Source of dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber promotes healthy digestion and helps maintain satiety.

items.title: Contains potassium
items.content: Potassium contributes to normal heart and muscle function.

items.title: Low in calories
items.content: Cooked kohlrabi fits well into calorie‑controlled diets.

items.title: Antioxidant compounds
items.content: Flavonoids and glucosinolates help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Gas and bloating
items.content: Like other cruciferous vegetables, kohlrabi can cause gas in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Thyroid interaction
items.content: Glucosinolates may affect thyroid function when consumed in excess.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Rarely, some people may experience an allergic reaction to kohlrabi.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Kohlrabi can be boiled until tender and added to soups, stews, or casseroles. It also works well sliced thin and quickly sautéed with olive oil and spices. Raw slices are suitable for salads, but the cooked version is milder and more aromatic.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store fresh kohlrabi in the refrigerator’s vegetable drawer, wrapped in a plastic bag, for up to 1 week. Cooked kohlrabi should be kept in an airtight container in the fridge and consumed within 3‑4 days.

pasta-with-tomato-based-sauce-meat-and-a.title: Pasta with tomato-based sauce, meat, and added vegetables

content.title: About
content.content: This is a home recipe for pasta cooked with a tomato‑based sauce, tender pieces of meat (usually beef or pork) and a mix of vegetables such as carrot, celery, bell pepper and zucchini. The pasta is boiled al dente, while the sauce, seasoned with basil, oregano and garlic, creates a rich, balanced flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Fresh tomato sauce is rich in lycopene, an antioxidant that supports heart health.
The tradition of pairing pasta with meat dates back to 19th‑century Italy, when meatballs became popular in sauce dishes.
Adding vegetables boosts fiber and vitamin content, making the dish more nutritious.
Durum‑wheat pasta has a lower glycemic index than soft‑wheat pasta.
Homemade tomato sauce retains more aromatic compounds than store‑bought canned versions.

items.title: Rich in antioxidants
items.content: Tomatoes provide lycopene and vitamin C, which help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Good source of protein
items.content: The meat supplies complete protein essential for tissue repair.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Vegetables like carrot and zucchini add dietary fiber that promotes regular bowel movements.

items.title: May lower cardiovascular risk
items.content: The combination of whole‑grain pasta, olive oil, and vegetables helps maintain healthy cholesterol levels.

items.title: Boosts immunity
items.content: Vitamins A and C from tomatoes and vegetables aid normal immune function.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: Wheat pasta contains gluten, which can trigger reactions in people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Using pre‑made tomato sauce or adding too much salt can make the dish overly salty.

items.title: Fatty meat
items.content: Fatty cuts increase calories and saturated fat; lean cuts are recommended.

items.title: Potential foodborne illness
items.content: Improperly stored leftovers or undercooked meat can harbor bacteria; refrigerate within 2 hours and consume within 2 days.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the pasta hot, sprinkled with grated Parmesan and fresh herbs such as parsley or basil. A pinch of red pepper flakes adds a gentle heat. It is eaten with a fork and spoon and pairs well with a glass of dry red wine.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. When reheating, add a splash of water or broth to prevent the sauce from drying out. The dish can be frozen for up to 2 months, preferably in individual portions.

content.title: About
content.content: A peanut butter and jelly sandwich consists of two slices of white bread with regular peanut butter and reduced‑sugar jelly spread evenly between them. It is a classic American snack known for its simplicity, the sweet‑salty flavor combination, and high energy content.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first commercial peanut butter and jelly sandwich recipe appeared in the United States in the early 1900s.
Peanut butter is a good source of plant protein and healthy fats.
Reducing sugar in the jelly lowers the glycemic index while preserving fruit flavor.
White bread is often chosen for its soft texture that holds the filling well.
The sandwich is a staple in school lunches and a quick snack for athletes.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Peanut butter provides about 25 g of protein per 100 g, supporting muscle maintenance.

items.title: Contains heart‑healthy monounsaturated fats
items.content: Monounsaturated fats in peanut butter can support cardiovascular health when consumed in moderation.

items.title: Lower‑sugar jelly
items.content: Reduced sugar helps minimize rapid blood‑glucose spikes.

items.title: Source of vitamin E
items.content: Peanut butter supplies vitamin E, an antioxidant that protects cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Provides sustained energy
items.content: The combination of carbohydrates from the bread and fats with protein offers lasting satiety and quick energy.

items.title: Peanut allergy
items.content: Peanut butter can trigger severe allergic reactions in sensitive individuals.

items.title: High calorie density
items.content: The sandwich contains roughly 350–400 kcal, so portion control is advisable for weight‑managed diets.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Some peanut butter varieties add salt; choose unsalted versions if you monitor sodium intake.

items.title: Gluten in bread
items.content: White bread contains gluten, which may be problematic for people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Spread a thin layer of peanut butter on one slice of bread, then evenly spread the reduced‑sugar jelly. Place the second slice on top, optionally cut the sandwich in half. It is convenient to eat by hand and can be served with fruit or vegetable sticks.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep a prepared sandwich in an airtight container at room temperature for no more than 4 hours. Store opened peanut butter and jelly in the refrigerator, and keep bread in a dry place or sealed bag to prevent drying out.

content.title: About
content.content: A white hoagie (submarine) roll is a soft, elongated wheat bun commonly used for sandwiches and burgers. The dough contains milk, butter, and a touch of sugar, giving it a mild flavor and a light, airy crumb.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The term “hoagie” originates from an American slang for a long sandwich.
White rolls are often chosen as a neutral base that lets the filling shine.
Traditionally they are baked at 190‑200 °C, producing a golden crust and a tender interior.
In some regions they are called “submarines” because of their boat‑like shape.
Variants may include sesame or poppy seeds for extra aroma.

items.title: Source of carbohydrates
items.content: The roll provides a quick source of energy through easily digestible carbs.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Enriched flour supplies thiamine, niacin, and folate, supporting metabolism.

items.title: Small amount of protein
items.content: While not a primary protein source, it contributes modestly to daily intake.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Iron, magnesium, and phosphorus are present, important for bones and blood formation.

items.title: Low fat content
items.content: Compared with baguettes or croissants, a white roll contains less fat when not topped with butter.

items.title: Gluten
items.content: Contains wheat, making it unsuitable for people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: Can raise blood sugar quickly, which may be undesirable for diabetics.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Salt is often added to the dough; those monitoring sodium should take this into account.

items.title: Dairy allergy
items.content: Milk and butter in the recipe can trigger reactions in dairy‑allergic individuals.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Use the roll as a base for sandwiches, burgers, hot subs, or appetizers. Slice it lengthwise, fill with meats, cheeses, vegetables, sauces, or toast it with butter for extra crispness.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep rolls in an airtight bag at room temperature for 2‑3 days. For longer storage, refrigerate up to a week or freeze for up to 3 months. Warm in the oven or toaster before serving to restore softness.
